profile.campus: Northlake, Cook County, Illinois (Microsoft Azure North Central US region)
profile.address: 601 Northwest Avenue, Northlake, Leyden Township, Cook County, Illinois, 60164
profile.reading:
This is Microsoft's data center in Northlake, Illinois, in the Chicago metro area, one of the company's earliest large-scale, purpose-built cloud facilities. Data Center Knowledge reported in November 2007 that Microsoft agreed to occupy a speculative 441,000-square-foot building on a 12-acre property that developers Ascent Corp. and the Koman Group, with Turner Construction managing the project, had begun building without a tenant already lined up. The facility was expected to cost more than $500 million and came with 40 megawatts of power available at 5 cents per kilowatt-hour, backed by a dedicated on-site substation. At the time, Microsoft was simultaneously operating a 470,000-square-foot data center in Quincy, Washington, and building a $550 million facility in San Antonio, part of a broader buildout as the company raced to expand internet infrastructure to compete with Google and other web-services rivals.

The Northlake facility now serves Microsoft's Azure North Central US region. A third-party data center aggregator has cited a roughly 120-megawatt capacity figure for the current Northlake campus, but Microsoft has not confirmed that number directly, and this registry treats it as an unverified lead rather than an operator-confirmed specification. Microsoft's own data center site publishes only aggregate worldwide statistics rather than per-facility details, so there is no current, operator-sourced power or square-footage figure to cite in its place. Because the original 2007 reporting is now nearly two decades old, this registry treats the 441,000-square-foot, $500 million, and 40 megawatt figures as historical facts about the facility's origin rather than a current specification, since Microsoft has not published whether or how the campus has since been expanded or upgraded.

ComEd, the electric utility serving the Chicago area, has cited large commercial and data center load growth in northeastern Illinois in its own distribution-planning filings with the Illinois Commerce Commission, part of a broader pattern across Midwest utilities adjusting long-range forecasts to account for hyperscale campuses like Microsoft's Northlake facility alongside newer entrants to the region. Northlake itself is a small, mostly industrial suburb west of Chicago along the Union Pacific rail corridor, and a hyperscale data center of this scale represents an unusually large single tenant for a town of its size, a pattern also seen in other Chicago-area suburbs such as Elk Grove Village and Aurora, Illinois, that have drawn large-format data center and industrial investment over the past two decades.

reading.body:
Microsoft's Northlake facility is a 441,000-square-foot campus in Cook County, Illinois that serves as part of the company's Azure North Central US region. Originally announced in 2007 as a 40-megawatt installation backed by a dedicated substation, it was one of Microsoft's early large-scale, purpose-built cloud data centers, built alongside contemporaneous hyperscale projects in Quincy, Washington and San Antonio, Texas as the company expanded to compete with Google in web services infrastructure. Microsoft has not published current capacity figures for the site, and this registry treats the original 2007 specifications as historical baseline rather than current confirmation.

A third-party aggregator has cited roughly 120 megawatts of capacity for the Northlake campus, but this figure is unverified by Microsoft directly. If accurate at that density, the campus would hold approximately 3,000 racks at a typical 40-kilowatt-per-rack AI training density, though this is an assumption rather than an operator claim. The actual current scale and composition of the facility remain unknown from published sources.

Illinois has 44 mapped data center facilities, of which only 6 publish power capacity figures totaling 236 megawatts across the state. Northlake ranks seventh among those six published figures, meaning it does not appear in the state's published capacity baseline, consistent with Microsoft's practice of disclosing only aggregate worldwide rather than per-facility statistics. ComEd, the Chicago-area utility, has cited large data center load growth in northeastern Illinois in its grid planning filings, naming hyperscale campuses like Northlake as part of the region's demand growth.
